# Mitsubishi Outlander Parasitic Draw Diagnosis

A parasitic draw of 280 milliamps in a modern vehicle like the Mitsubishi Outlander is significant enough to deplete a standard lead-acid battery within a day or two, even after charging. You correctly identified that pulling the Input/Output Distribution (IOD) fuse terminated the draw entirely. This specific result isolates your investigation to the circuits protected by that single fuse. The fact that you latched the hood and kept the key fob distant confirms you've eliminated obvious external triggers like the hood switch or remote entry system, which is a good start to ruling out intermittent faults.

In automotive electrical systems, the IOD fuse acts as the master gatekeeper for most accessory power domains. On many Mitsubishi platforms, this fuse protects modules critical to vehicle operation when parked, including the Engine Control Module (ECM), Transmission Control Module (TCM), Body Control Module (BCM), and various relay drivers that control the alternator or starter solenoid. The issue isn't necessarily a short circuit causing massive current flow; it is often a module failing to enter sleep mode, leaving internal clocks or diagnostic buses active.

To pinpoint the culprit without blindly removing fuses one by oneâwhich risks damaging sensitive electronics if you accidentally isolate a module that needs to remain powered for calibrationâyou need a methodical approach using an ammeter and fuse isolation. Since pulling the IOD fuse killed the draw, your next step is to determine which specific sub-circuit within that fuse's domain is active.

You can achieve this by removing the IOD fuse and inserting it into the positive lead of a digital multimeter set to measure DC amps in series with the battery. Alternatively, if you have access to a fused jumper wire rated for at least 10 amps and your multimeter has high-current capability, you can bypass the fuse entirely while monitoring current. However, the safest and most precise method involves installing an inline ammeter between the battery positive terminal and the IOD fuse holder. This allows you to monitor the draw in real-time while you systematically isolate other fuses downstream of the IOD circuit.

Start by removing one fuse at a time from the main distribution box (usually located under the dashboard or in the engine bay) that is not essential for basic safety systems like ABS or SRS airbags, as those should generally remain powered even when the vehicle is off. Watch your multimeter reading. When you remove a specific fuse and the amperage drops significantly, you have identified the circuit responsible for the excess draw.

Once you identify the offending fuse, inspect the corresponding component. Common culprits in the Outlander include a malfunctioning BCM that fails to sleep, a stuck relay (often found near the battery or under the hood), or a shorted wire within an aftermarket accessory like an alarm system or remote start unit connected to the IOD circuit. If the vehicle has an aftermarket stereo or camera system installed, ensure their ignition sense wires are properly grounded and not constantly pulling power.

It is also worth noting your observation regarding the battery voltage drop of 1/4 volt per day. While a new battery should hold charge longer, a consistent drain indicates that the load exceeds the alternator's ability to replenish the battery while parked. If you isolate the circuit but cannot find a physical short, the issue may lie within the module's firmware or internal logic. In such cases, updating the vehicle's software at a dealership or specialized shop might resolve a known bug causing the module to wake up unnecessarily.

If no specific fuse removal reduces the draw after isolating all non-essential circuits, the problem likely lies within the IOD fuse box itself, possibly due to a shorted ground wire inside the fuse block or a failed internal connection on the main feed. Always verify your battery health again after resolving the draw issue; even with the draw fixed, a battery that has been deeply discharged may suffer from sulfation unless it was professionally reconditioned.
